newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain and US to resume open skies talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain and US to resume open skies talks.

text.p: Britain said on Wednesday that it is to resume stalled "open skies" trade talks with the United States next week, aimed at opening up the trans-Atlantic air travel market to free competition.
An official at the Department of Transport said its negotiators would be meeting their U.S. counterparts for a two-day session in Washington on November 6-7.
"They are taking place at the US's request following informal contacts after the last round of talks (in August) was cancelled," he said.

The news sparked fresh industry speculation that a compromise deal is now in the offing after months of deadlock, which would also open the way for British Airways and American Airlines to win approval for their controversial plans to join forces on the transatlantic market.
Shares in British Airways rose nine pence to 563-1/2 on renewed optimism that the deal with American can get approval, analysts said.
Britain is believed to have now put off a long awaited ruling on the proposed alliance until mid-November, airline industry sources said.

The industry has been waiting for trade minister Ian Lang to decide whether or not to block the deal ever since his Office of Fair Trading (OFT) completed an investigation into the competition issues on September 17.
But Lang has now stepped back from making any immediate decision to make way for the new round of open skies talks, several airline executives said.
Lang's Department of Trade and Industry routinely declines to comment on when he might announce his decision.

The fresh attempt at agreeing an "open skies" deal began in July after British Airways and American urged the governments to free up competition as a necessary precondition for their joint marketing agreement.
However, airline executives said it was too early to say whether the two governments can now reach agreement on open skies, having failed repeatedly in a long saga of talks dating back to 1991.
"This is a surprising twist in that the talks are back on again but I still think there is a long way to go," said an executive with one U.S. airline.
The U.S. Department of Transportation broke off the last round of talks in August because of the lack of progress.

Washington has made any approval of the BA/American alliance conditional on getting open skies with Britain, and in particular in getting open access for all U.S. carriers to London's Heathrow, Europe's most popular airport.

But rival U.S. and British carriers say Heathrow is so overcrowded that open access would be meaningless unless they were to be granted some of British Airways' 38 percent share of existing takeoff and landing slots.

Industry sources said if next week's talks in Washington go well, a second round of talks in London has been pencilled in by negotiators and airline lobbyists for the week of November 18, the same week in which Lang is now expected to make his ruling.
